title: Solve decimal addition and subtraction problems with money and metric measures

lesson.title: Money and Metres: Decimals in Real Life

steps.say: You already know how to line up the decimal points and add or subtract carefully. Today we learn how to spot when a real story, like buying a snack at the store, is secretly asking you to do exactly that.

Here is the trick. When a story puts amounts together, that is adding. When a story asks what is left over, or how much change you get, that is subtracting. Let us look at a real one. At a shop in Victoria, a smoothie costs four dollars and seventy-five cents, and a granola bar costs two dollars and thirty-five cents. The words put them together, so this is adding.

visual.caption: Two prices joining together means we add

steps.say: So we line up the decimal points and add. Five hundredths plus five hundredths makes ten hundredths, so we write a zero and carry one. Seven tenths plus three tenths plus that carried one makes eleven tenths, so we write one tenth and carry one whole. Four plus two plus one is seven. The total is seven dollars and ten cents.

visual.caption: Starting at 4.75 and hopping 2.35 more lands on 7.10

steps.say: Now you hand the cashier a ten dollar bill. How much change comes back? That is the leftover part, so we subtract. Write ten dollars as ten point zero zero, then take away seven dollars and ten cents. Ten minus seven point one zero is two dollars and ninety cents.

visual.caption: The whole ten dollars splits into the cost and the change

steps.say: Here is the slip lots of kids make. They write ten with no decimal, then squish the numbers to the right, like ten under seven point one zero, and they get something silly like three dollars and ninety cents. Ten dollars is really ten point zero zero. Fill the empty spots with zeros so every place lines up, and the change is two dollars and ninety cents. The same idea works with metres and litres, so one point five metres is really one point five zero zero metres.

visual.caption: Ten dollars has empty tenths and hundredths — fill them with zeros

steps.say: So whenever a money or measuring story shows up, ask yourself one question first: am I putting amounts together, or finding what is left? Then line up those decimal points and go.

lesson.answer: Together means add, what is left means subtract — then line up the decimal points and fill the gaps with zeros.

practice.question: Nadia takes her water bottle to soccer practice in Burnaby. It holds 0.750 litres of water, and during the game she drinks 0.425 litres. How much water is still in her bottle? Try drawing a bar for the whole 0.750 litres and splitting it into the part she drank and the part left.
practice.answer: 0.325 litres are left. She is finding what is left, so she subtracts: 0.750 minus 0.425 equals 0.325 litres.
